ancient.name: Sima de los Huesos
ancient.story_individual:
Around 400,000 years ago, a hominin died and their remains ended up in what would become known as Sima de los Huesos (Pit of Bones) in northern Spain. The individual's remains, including a femur which would later yield crucial DNA evidence, were preserved alongside approximately 28 other individuals in the cave system at Atapuerca. While researchers cannot determine this individual's biological sex, they know they belonged to a population that showed Neanderthal-like features in their skeletal morphology.

The remarkable preservation of their DNA was made possible by the stable, cold conditions within the cave. When the femur was analyzed in 2014, the DNA retrieved from it represented the oldest human DNA ever sequenced, pushing back the boundaries of ancient DNA research by hundreds of thousands of years. The mitochondrial DNA unexpectedly showed closer affinity to Denisovans than to Neanderthals, despite the skeletal characteristics of the population.

The recovery of such ancient DNA was a major technical achievement that required innovative methods to deal with highly degraded genetic material. While we don't know the details of this individual's life - what they ate, how they lived, or how they died - their genetic legacy has provided crucial insights into human evolution and the complex relationships between ancient hominin populations.

Subsequent nuclear DNA analysis of Sima de los Huesos hominins revealed a closer connection to Neanderthals than the mtDNA initially suggested, adding another fascinating layer to this individual's story.

References

  • Meyer, M., Fu, Q., Aximu-Petri, A. et al. A mitochondrial genome sequence of a hominin from Sima de los Huesos. Nature 505, 403–406 (2014). https://doi.org/10.1038/nature12788

  • Meyer, M., Arsuaga, JL., de Filippo, C. et al. Nuclear DNA sequences from the Middle Pleistocene Sima de los Huesos hominins. Nature 531, 504–507 (2016). https://doi.org/10.1038/nature17405

Pictured: Cranium 17 of the Sima de los Huesos, from an individual from the same location and time period. Nohemi Sala, Juan Luis Arsuaga, Ana Pantoja-Pérez, Adrián Pablos, Ignacio Martínez, Rolf M. Quam, Asier Gómez-Olivencia, José María Bermúdez de Castro, Eudald Carbonell, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

famous.name: Philip Davis
famous.story_individual:
Philip Edward “Brave” Davis is the 5th Prime Minister of The Bahamas and the longstanding Member of Parliament for Cat Island, Rum Cay and San Salvador. Born into modest circumstances as the son of a taxi driver and a hotel maid, Davis was raised mainly by his grandparents, who together instilled in him discipline, resilience, and a strong work ethic. From the age of seven, Davis worked odd jobs to help support his family, later following his grandfather into construction before pursuing a legal career.

Davis’ path to law is a testament to determination and self-discipline. He did not attend a traditional law school. Instead, he qualified through the British professional legal training system, relying on self-directed study and examinations. He went on to establish a highly respected legal career, serving as a long-term partner at the firm Christie, Ingraham and Co., which later became Davis and Co. His appointment as King’s Counsel recognized his standing as one of the country’s leading attorneys.

His public service spans decades and includes roles as Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Works and Urban Development. In 2017, he became Leader of the Progressive Liberal Party, and in 2021, he led the PLP to a national election victory. As Prime Minister, Davis has prioritized economic recovery, climate resilience, social protection, and strengthening the global presence of The Bahamas. Known for his people-centred leadership and deep empathy for working families, he continues to champion opportunity, dignity, and sustainable development across the archipelago.

Davis is also a participant in the ongoing Genetic Legacy of the Transatlantic Slave Trade project, which is examining ancestral connections among Bahamians from islands such as New Providence and Cat Island. His participation reflects his commitment to understanding and preserving Bahamian heritage. Notably, he was the first volunteer to donate a DNA sample from Cat Island, personally contributing to the effort to map and celebrate the deep ancestral roots of the Bahamian people.

Biography written by Dr. Michael Pateman. Pictured: Philip Davis in 2022 by Palácio do Planalto from Brasilia, Brasil, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

famous.name: Zana
famous.story_individual:
Zana was a woman who lived in the 19th century in Abkhazia, a region in the South Caucasus. She became a subject of local folklore and later scientific interest due to her unusual appearance and behavior. Zana’s origins are uncertain but she was enslaved by local nobles, and eventually came into the possession of an Abkhaz nobleman named Edgi Genaba.

According to local accounts, Zana was described as being unusually tall (around 2 meters), dark-skinned, and covered with thick hair. She was said to possess extraordinary strength, capable of outrunning a horse and lifting heavy weights with ease. Zana was unable to speak and exhibited behavior that the local people considered wild or animalistic, leading some to refer to her as an "Almasty" - a local term similar to Bigfoot or Yeti.

Despite her captive status, Zana bore several children to local men, including her son Khwit. She reportedly had two sons and two daughters in total. Zana lived on the Genaba estate in Tkhina until her death, which occurred around 1890.

Zana’s descendants. Top panel: Her daughter Kodzhanar and son Khwit. Bottom panel: Khwit’s children, from left to right: Tanya, Raya, Shaliko. Margaryan et al. 2021 (Supplementary Figure S1.1), CC-BY-4.0.

For many years, there was speculation about Zana's origins, with some suggesting she might represent a remnant population of archaic humans. However, genetic studies conducted in the 21st century, particularly a 2021 study by Margaryan et al., revealed that Zana's ancestry could be traced to East African populations. The researchers speculated that she might have had a genetic condition such as congenital generalized hypertrichosis, which could explain her unusual appearance and some of her reported behaviors.

Face reconstruction from Zana’s skull (top left) by G. Lebedinskaya (1976). Bottom right – artistic reconstruction by amateur artist Roman Moskalik after consideration of witness accounts (2013). Margaryan et al. 2021 (Supplementary Figure S1.5), CC-BY-4.0.

Zana's life story highlights the complex interplay between folklore, scientific inquiry, and the treatment of individuals perceived as "different" in 19th century society. Her experiences and the subsequent scientific investigations of her remains and those of her descendants have contributed significantly to our understanding of human diversity and the power of genomic research in unraveling historical mysteries.

References

  • Margaryan A, Sinding M-HS, Carøe C, Yamshchikov V, Burtsev I, Gilbert MTP. The genomic origin of Zana of Abkhazia. Advanced Genetics. 2021; 2(2):e10051. https://doi.org/10.1002/ggn2.10051

Pictured: Artistic reconstruction of Zana by amateur artist Roman Moskalik based on the forensic reconstruction by G. Lebedinskaya and witness accounts (2013). Margaryan et al. 2021 (Supplementary Figure S1.5), CC-BY-4.0. Biography in part generated using Anthropic (2024) Claude 3.5 Sonnet [Large language model].

famous.name: Khwit
famous.story_individual:
Khwit was born between 1884 and 1889 in Abkhazia, a region in the South Caucasus. He was the son of Zana, a mysterious woman of uncertain origins who had been enslaved by local nobles. Zana was the subject of much local folklore due to her unusual appearance and behavior. She was unusually tall (around 2 meters), dark-skinned, covered with thick hair, and unable to speak. There were rumors that Khwit's father was Edgi Genaba, the nobleman who kept Zana enslaved.

Unlike his mother, Khwit was able to integrate into the local community, though he was known for his distinctive appearance and extraordinary strength. He had more African features than the local population, but his hair was straight and stiff. Khwit was described as extremely strong and was known to be quick to pick fights. In one such altercation, he lost his right hand, but this didn't hinder his ability to work on a collective farm or even climb trees using just his left hand.

Khwit married twice in his lifetime. From his first marriage, he had a daughter named Tanya. His second marriage produced two more children: a daughter, Raya, and a son, Shaliko.

Khwit and his family. Top panel: His sister Kodzhanar and Khwit. Bottom panel: Khwit’s children, from left to right: Tanya, Raya, Shaliko. Margaryan et al. 2021 (Supplementary Figure S1.1), CC-BY-4.0.

Despite his challenging beginnings, Khwit lived a full life in his community. He died in 1954 at the age of 65-70 and was buried in the Genaba family cemetery, possibly next to his mother Zana. His grave became a focal point for researchers interested in the story of Zana and the possibility of unusual human populations in the Caucasus region.

After his death, Khwit's remains were exhumed for scientific study. Genetic testing performed on his remains, particularly the 2021 genomic analysis by Margaryan et al., confirmed that Khwit was indeed Zana's son and that his genetic ancestry was a mix of East African (from his mother) and local Abkhazian (likely from his father) origins.

Khwit's life and the scientific investigations that followed his death have played a crucial role in unraveling the mystery surrounding his mother, Zana, and in demonstrating how modern scientific techniques can be used to investigate historical and folkloric claims.

References

  • Margaryan A, Sinding M-HS, Carøe C, Yamshchikov V, Burtsev I, Gilbert MTP. The genomic origin of Zana of Abkhazia. Advanced Genetics. 2021; 2(2):e10051. https://doi.org/10.1002/ggn2.10051

famous.name: Neanderthal Man
famous.story_individual:
Neanderthals were first named and unearthed in 1856 in the Neander Valley of Germany, three full years before Darwin published his book On the Origin of Species. In his writings, Darwin only briefly wrote about human evolution and did not mention anything about the newly named Neanderthals. Coincidentally, by 1848, a Neanderthal skeleton had already been discovered in Gibraltar. That specimen, however, had remained uncharacterized in science. So, as fate would have it, the German team is credited with discovering the new species, and the name Neanderthal still remains. Neanderthal Man (seen pictured as a reconstruction) from Feldhofer cave in Neander Valley lived approximately 40,000 years ago.

Today, we know much more about these cousins of Homo sapiens (humans), when and where they lived and how they may have mated with our stone-age ancestors. In 2008, a team led by Nobel Laureate Svante Pääbo sequenced the first Neanderthal genome, and just months after that publication, anthropologists discovered that Neanderthal DNA still resided in most humans alive today. Yes, humans and Neanderthals had mated.

Although the common evolutionary ancestor to Homo sapiens and Neanderthals lived more than half-a-million years ago, we now know that the Y chromosome of the male Neanderthals sequenced to date came from an introduction event (a mating) between a male archaic human and a female Neanderthal between 370,000 and 100,000 years ago. This, and other new findings, suggests that mixing between human ancestors and Neanderthals occurred early and possibly frequently while they co-existed for millennia in Europe and Asia, which was until approximately 35,000 years ago when Neanderthals went extinct. 

We are fortunate to be living in an amazing time where every year new discoveries add exciting information about humans, our ancestors, and our shared prehistory. The last decade alone has completely reshaped our knowledge and relationship with the once mighty Neanderthals.

Homo neanderthalensis reconstruction - Mr. N

©Neanderthal Museum
